Fictive means belonging to, created by, or relating to imagination rather than reality. If something is fictive, it was invented — it does not exist in the real world, only in the mind or in a story.

Think of it as a label that signals: "This thing was made up."

"Fictive" works in three related but slightly different ways depending on how it's used. Understanding all three will give you complete command of the word.

Shade 1: Imagined, invented, not real

This is the most common use. A fictive thing is one that was created by someone's imagination — it has no existence outside of a story, a narrative, or a mental invention.

  • A fictive world is a world that lives only inside a novel or film — it was built by an author's imagination, not discovered in real life.
  • A fictive character is someone an author invented, not a real person.
  • A fictive narrative is a story that was made up.

In this sense, "fictive" is very close in meaning to "fictional." You could often swap one for the other and mean roughly the same thing. The word simply signals: this is not from reality; it came from imagination.

Shade 2: Relating to the power or act of creating fiction

Here, "fictive" doesn't just label the product of imagination — it describes the faculty, ability, or process of imagination itself.

  • A writer's fictive imagination refers to their mental power to invent stories, create characters, and build worlds from nothing.
  • A fictive gift would mean a natural talent for creating fiction.
  • Fictive creation refers to the act of constructing something imagined.

In this sense, "fictive" is more active — it points to the making of fiction, not just the thing that was made. Think of it as describing the engine (imagination) rather than just the car (the story).

Shade 3: Assumed, pretended, or treated as real when it isn't (technical use)

This is the most specialized meaning, common in academic fields like anthropology, sociology, and law. Here, something fictive is something that doesn't genuinely exist as what it claims to be, but is deliberately assumed or treated as if it does, for practical or social purposes.

The clearest example is fictive kinship. This is when two people treat each other as family — say, calling a close family friend "Uncle Ray" or "Auntie Sue" — even though there is no actual blood relationship or legal adoption connecting them. The relationship is treated as if it were family, even though technically it isn't. Anthropologists call this fictive kinship.

Another example: in legal reasoning, a fictive assumption is a premise that everyone knows isn't literally true, but that the legal system treats as true in order to make a rule work fairly. The fiction is admitted, but used on purpose.

So in this shade, "fictive" means: deliberately assumed or constructed, with everyone aware it isn't strictly real, but accepted and treated as real for a specific purpose.
How "fictive" is different from similar words

Since "fictive," "fictional," and "fictitious" all look and sound similar, it helps to know exactly how they differ.

Fictional is the most general and neutral of the three. It simply means "from or relating to fiction." A fictional character is a character in a story — straightforward, no extra baggage.

Fictive carries more weight. It can mean fictional, but it also suggests the act of imagining and creating, and it has that third, technical meaning of "assumed/pretended but treated as real." It is a more precise and loaded word, used in more formal or academic settings.

Fictitious leans more strongly toward false or not genuine, and often carries a negative or suspicious tone — as if someone is deliberately pretending something is real when it isn't, possibly to deceive. A fictitious name is a fake name. A fictitious claim is a false claim. Where "fictive" is neutral and even admiring (a writer's fictive imagination is a good thing), "fictitious" often implies dishonesty or fraud.

A quick way to hold them apart:

  • Fictional → exists in fiction / from a story
  • Fictive → imaginatively created; or assumed-as-real for a purpose (technical)
  • Fictitious → false, fake, not genuine (often with a negative edge)
Who uses this word and where

"Fictive" is not a word you'll hear in casual everyday conversation. It lives in formal, literary, and academic language. You are most likely to encounter it in:

  • Literary criticism — when scholars discuss the invented world of a novel or the imaginative power of an author ("the fictive landscape of the story")
  • Anthropology and sociology — when discussing social relationships that function like real ones but aren't ("fictive kinship")
  • Philosophy and legal theory — when discussing assumed premises that are treated as true ("a fictive legal construct")

In plain speech, most people would just say "fictional," "made-up," or "imaginary." When you see "fictive," you know the writer is being deliberate and precise.

Fictive is an adjective with one root idea — produced by imagination rather than reality — that branches in three directions: (1) simply describing something as invented or imagined, (2) describing the creative power of imagination itself, and (3) describing something deliberately assumed or treated as real even though it technically isn't. It is a formal, precise word that you'll find in literary, academic, and technical contexts, and it sits between the simplicity of "fictional" and the negative charge of "fictitious."
